it-load.d: The total electrical power drawn by the IT equipment itself — servers, storage arrays, and network devices — excluding cooling and power-delivery overhead. It is the sizing anchor for the whole facility: cooling capacity, UPS, generators, and Total CAPEX all scale from it, and PUE is defined relative to it. Small/edge sites run 100–500 kW, hyperscale campuses exceed 10 MW; the capex calculator accepts 100 kW to 100 MW.

fuel-autonomy.d: How long the backup generators can run at full facility load without refueling during a utility outage. It is driven by on-site tank capacity versus generator fuel burn, and it directly supports the Tier classification: Uptime Institute Tier III expects 48 hours minimum, while mission-critical sites carry 72+ hours plus refueling contracts. More autonomy means larger tanks, more fuel-polishing systems, and higher Generator Type CAPEX.

building-type.d: The type of structure that houses the data hall, which swings construction cost by a factor of two. Warehouse conversions are cheapest (0.70x) because the shell exists; modular/prefab runs 0.85x with faster schedules; purpose-built is the 1.00x baseline optimized for load paths, floor loading, and cooling; high-rise multi-story is costliest (1.40x) due to structural steel, vertical riser distribution, and craneage. The choice also shifts build time (modular ~0.6x, high-rise ~1.4x of baseline schedule), which interacts with Year Escalation.

seismic-zone.d: The earthquake-risk classification of the site, which dictates structural reinforcement: base isolation, braced racks, seismically rated cable tray and piping restraints. Cost impact ranges from +0% in Zone 0 to +15% in Zone 4 (very high risk); Indonesia is typically Zone 2–4. It also affects equipment anchorage specs for UPS Type and Generator Type gear and feeds the Disaster Risk assessment.

rack-density.d: Power consumption per rack, the single strongest driver of the cooling architecture. Standard racks at 5–7 kW are fine on air cooling; 10–15 kW needs enhanced airflow or in-row units; 20–30 kW requires in-row or rear-door heat exchangers (RDHX); AI/HPC racks at 50–100 kW demand direct liquid cooling (DLC). Higher density shrinks White Space per megawatt but concentrates heat, raising Cooling Type CAPEX per rack while lowering building cost per kW.

cooling-type.d: The heat-rejection technology, which affects both CAPEX and operational efficiency (PUE). Air cooling via CRAC/CRAH units serves standard racks under 10 kW; in-row precision units handle 10–20 kW; RDHX (rear-door heat exchangers) cover 20–40 kW; DLC (direct liquid cooling) is required for AI/HPC racks at 50+ kW. The choice sets the Refrigerant path (chiller/CRAC vs chiller-less), the achievable PUE, and build schedule (liquid ~1.3x, Deep Sea Water Cooling ~1.45x of baseline cooling schedule).

redundancy.d: How many spare capacity paths the power and cooling systems carry: N is need-only, N+1 adds one spare module, 2N duplicates the entire plant, 2N+1 duplicates plus a spare. Higher redundancy buys uptime — N gives 99.671% (~28.8 hr/yr down), N+1 gives 99.982% (~1.6 hr/yr), 2N gives 99.995% (~26 min/yr) — but 2N roughly doubles the electrical and mechanical infrastructure cost. Redundancy is the primary determinant of the Tier Classification and Expected Uptime shown in the results.

fire-suppression.d: Clean-agent suppression systems designed to extinguish fire without damaging live IT equipment (no water dump on servers). FM200/HFC-227ea is common but being phased out on GWP grounds; Novec 1230 is the low-GWP, safest mainstream choice; Inergen (IG-541) is an inert-gas system with no residue; nitrogen inerting suits permanently sealed rooms; water mist is the green alternative for support spaces. Works alongside the Fire Alarm System — detection triggers release, so early VESDA sensing reduces discharge events.

fire-alarm.d: The detection layer that triggers Fire Suppression — in a data center, minutes of early warning are worth millions in avoided discharge and downtime. Conventional systems detect late-stage smoke only; addressable systems identify the exact point location; VESDA (aspirating smoke detection) continuously samples air and catches pre-combustion particles before visible smoke; hybrid VESDA + addressable combines earliest warning with precise location. Tier III+ facilities typically specify VESDA in white space.

ups-type.d: The battery/rotary system that bridges the 10–15 second gap between a utility outage and generator pickup — the heartbeat of ride-through power. Standalone units suit small fixed capacity; modular UPS scales in blocks and can carry N+1 within the frame; distributed/rack UPS fits edge deployments; rotary (diesel-coupled flywheel) UPS is the ultra-reliable option that merges UPS and generator. The choice interacts with Redundancy topology (N+1 vs 2N paths) and on-site BESS, which can double as UPS reserve.

generator-type.d: The backup power generation fuel choice, affecting maintenance regime, emissions, and sustainability posture. Diesel is the reliable industry standard; natural gas cuts local emissions but depends on pipeline availability during regional events; dual-fuel offers flexibility; HVO/biodiesel achieves roughly 90% lower lifecycle CO2 and is a drop-in decarbonization lever that improves the Carbon/ESG picture. Sizing pairs with Fuel Autonomy (tank hours) and Redundancy (N+1 or 2N generator sets).

region-location.d: The geographic region that sets the base construction-cost multiplier before any city-level override: Americas is the 1.00x baseline, EMEA-Europe runs 1.15x, Middle East 0.90x, and APAC averages 0.85x but varies widely (Tokyo and Singapore are among the world's most expensive markets). Region also drives permitting timelines and labor market conditions. Selecting a specific City / Market replaces this generic multiplier with precise $/W data from Turner & Townsend DCCI 2025 and Cushman & Wakefield 2025.

city-market.d: Metro-level construction cost per watt of IT capacity, which overrides the generic Region multiplier with published market data. The spread is large: Tokyo ~$15.20/W and Zurich ~$14.50/W at the top, Dallas ~$14.30/W, down to Warsaw ~$9.00/W and Chennai ~$6.20/W. Cost per Watt is the industry's headline benchmarking unit and maps directly to Cost per kW (multiply by 1,000). Sources: Turner & Townsend DCCI 2025, Cushman & Wakefield 2025.

year-escalation.d: Multi-year construction cost inflation applied to future project start dates. Data center construction ran ~7% CAGR from 2020–2025 (Turner & Townsend) driven by equipment lead times and labor scarcity, and is projected to decelerate as supply chains normalize: 2026 +6.0%, 2027 cumulative 1.115x, through 2030 at 1.250x of the 2025 baseline. Escalation compounds with build duration, so slower Building Type or Delivery Method choices absorb more of it.
year-escalation.s: JLL 2026 Outlook, Turner & Townsend DCCI 2025, Avid Solutions 2026-2030 projections

front-of-meter.d: Grid-side infrastructure the operator often pays for under the utility agreement even though it sits before the revenue meter: interconnection, Substation, transformer, and switchgear, plus the utility's regulated Rate of Return (typically ~9%) on that investment. These costs are frequently forgotten in early budgets yet can add millions — 'Don't forget front-of-meter: transformer, substation, switchgear, and the utility's 9% return on investment' (Mark Lewis, VP Engineering). Transformer Lead Time (18–36 months) often gates the whole project schedule.

substation-type.d: The grid connection point sizing. A shared utility substation costs $0.5–1.5M but caps capacity and expansion; a dedicated 33kV substation ($3–5M) is typical for 5–30 MW campuses; dedicated 132kV+ ($5–10M+) is required for hyperscale loads and gives the operator control over reliability. Part of the Front-of-Meter cost block, and the voltage class drives Transformer Lead Time exposure.

transformer-lead.d: The procurement wait for large power transformers, currently one of the industry's worst supply-chain bottlenecks. Standard delivery is 18–24 months; extended market conditions push 24–36 months and add ~15% cost; emergency expedited procurement adds ~30%. Because the transformer often sits on the project critical path, lead time interacts with Year Escalation (longer builds absorb more inflation) and can dominate the Capacity Plan timeline.

utility-rate.d: The regulated return (typically 7–12%, commonly ~9%) a utility earns on Front-of-Meter infrastructure it builds on the operator's behalf, passed through in the interconnection agreement or tariff. A higher allowed return raises the effective cost of grid-supplied capacity and can tip the economics toward On-Site Renewables or a dedicated Substation owned outright.

market-condition.d: Current supply-demand dynamics in the construction market at bid time. In a buyer's market (overcapacity) pricing drops ~5%; balanced is the baseline; in a seller's market — the norm during the AI build-out — contractors charge ~+10% premiums because order books are full. Compounds with Contractor Availability and Year Escalation; timing a bid into a cooler market is one of the few free CAPEX levers.

delivery-method.d: The contracting structure for design and construction, which shifts both cost and risk allocation. Design-Bid-Build is the baseline (full owner control, sequential schedule); Design-Build integrates the two and saves ~3%; modular-prefab moves work into the factory for ~-8% and faster schedules; EPC turnkey costs ~+5% for single-source responsibility but transfers delivery risk to the contractor. The right choice depends on the owner's in-house Project Management capability and risk appetite.

contractor-availability.d: Labor-market tightness in the chosen metro, a major source of regional cost variance — location-specific labor costs drive significant spread between otherwise identical builds (per Matt Pacione). High availability adds no premium, normal markets ~+3%, and tight markets (multiple hyperscale projects competing for the same electricians and pipefitters) ~+8%. Correlates strongly with Market Conditions and the City / Market cost level.

design-fee.d: Architecture, MEP engineering, and specialty consulting fees, typically 5–12% of construction cost (8% is a common midpoint for mission-critical work, higher than commercial buildings because of redundancy engineering and commissioning documentation). Complex Cooling Type choices (DLC, Deep Sea Water Cooling) and high Redundancy push toward the top of the range. Booked as a soft cost alongside the Project Management fee and Contingency.

pm-fee.d: Owner's project management and construction management cost, typically 3–8% of construction value (5% midpoint). Covers schedule control, vendor coordination, quality assurance, and commissioning oversight — cheap insurance on a project where a missed Transformer Lead Time or failed integrated systems test costs far more. Lower when using EPC turnkey Delivery Method (contractor absorbs coordination), higher for multi-phase Capacity Plan builds.

contingency.d: The budget reserve for unknowns — design development, scope growth, market movement, and site surprises — typically 5–20% of estimated cost (10% is standard for well-defined projects; early-stage or novel-technology builds like Deep Sea Water Cooling carry 15%+). Contingency is exactly what the Monte-Carlo P10/P50/P90 range quantifies: if your P90 sits far above your point estimate, your contingency is telling you it is too thin.

power-distribution.d: How power travels from switchgear to the PDUs on the floor. Overhead cable tray is cheapest (-8%) but less flexible for moves and changes; busway (busbar trunking) is the industry-standard baseline for large facilities with tap-off flexibility; underground conduit adds ~+15% for cable pits and trenching but suits campus layouts; mixed bus + underground (+8%) fits multi-building sites. Interacts with Floor Construction (underfloor routing needs raised floor).

transformer-type.d: The medium-voltage to low-voltage step-down transformer construction. Oil-filled outdoor units are ~10% cheaper but require oil containment bunds and fire separation distances; dry-type is the standard indoor choice; cast-resin is the premium indoor option (+12%) with the lowest fire risk and best tolerance of humid or dusty environments. Distinct from the large grid transformers counted under Front-of-Meter.

pdu-type.d: The rack-level power strips that feed servers. Basic metered PDUs (~$800/rack) only distribute and show aggregate load; intelligent monitored PDUs (~$1,500/rack) add per-outlet metering feeding DCIM/CBM analytics; intelligent + switched (~$2,500/rack) adds remote outlet control for stranded-capacity recovery and remote reboot. Per-outlet visibility becomes critical at high Rack Density where a single overloaded circuit can trip a whole AI pod.

cabling-type.d: Backbone and horizontal network cabling. Cat6A copper (~$600/rack) suits standard enterprise; hybrid fiber backbone + Cat6A drops (~$1,200/rack) is the mainstream standard; all-fiber OM4/OS2 (~$2,000/rack) is the premium choice for high-density and AI facilities where 400G+ east-west fabrics dominate. AI clusters can spend more on optics and cabling per rack than on power distribution, so density strategy (Rack Density) drives this line item.

floor-type.d: Whether the data hall uses an access (raised) floor or slab-on-grade with overhead services. Raised floor enables under-floor air distribution and cable routing but adds $25–50/sqft; 600 mm is the baseline, 900 mm adds ~+6% and 1200 mm ~+12% on the building for high-airflow designs. Slab with overhead distribution saves ~5% and is increasingly popular for high Rack Density deployments where air comes from in-row or liquid loops rather than under the floor.

site-condition.d: The starting state of the land or building. Greenfield (raw land) adds +5–8% for grading, drainage, and utility extensions; brownfield (existing industrial site) is the baseline needing some demolition; retrofit/conversion of an existing building adds +10–20% for demolition, structural adaptation, and working around as-built surprises. Interacts with Building Type — a warehouse conversion is by definition a retrofit play trading shell savings against adaptation cost.

security-level.d: The physical security infrastructure package: fencing, CCTV, access control, bollards, mantraps, vehicle barriers, and a security operations center (SOC). Standard (CCTV + access control) is baseline; enterprise adds ~+2% for biometrics and mantraps; high security adds ~+5% for a 24/7 SOC, anti-vehicle K12 barriers, and layered perimeters. Colocation and Hyperscaler Pre-Lease customers frequently mandate specific levels, and Compliance regimes (SOC 2, ISO 27001) audit against them.

fiber-entry.d: The number of physically diverse fiber paths into the building. A single path (~$150K) is a single point of failure; dual diverse entry (~$350K) is the standard for Tier III+ so one backhoe cannot sever connectivity; multi-path with a carrier meet-me room (~$600K) adds interconnection revenue potential and carrier density that raises Colocation Pricing power. Network diversity mirrors the power Redundancy philosophy — no single point of failure.

green-certification.d: Third-party green building certification, adding 2–8% to construction cost for sustainable materials, energy modeling, enhanced commissioning, and documentation: LEED Silver ~+2%, Gold ~+4%, Platinum ~+8% (BREEAM Very Good/Outstanding are the European equivalents). The premium buys lower long-term OPEX (better PUE and WUE by design), easier permitting in strict jurisdictions, and ESG credibility that Hyperscaler Pre-Lease tenants increasingly require.

onsite-renewable.d: On-site solar PV and/or battery energy storage (BESS) reducing grid dependency at the cost of added CAPEX: rooftop solar runs roughly $1.2M/MW installed, solar + BESS roughly $2.5M/MW. BESS (screening basis ~$180/kWh installed, ~88% round-trip efficiency) can double as UPS reserve and peak-shaving asset. On-site generation improves CUE (carbon intensity) and hedges the electricity rate behind the Annual Energy Cost, but land take (~1.2 ha/MWp for solar) usually caps it well below full facility load.

total-capex.d: The total upfront investment required to build the data center: construction, electrical and mechanical equipment, fit-out, soft costs (Design Fee, Project Management, Contingency), and commissioning. It scales primarily with IT Load, Redundancy, Cooling Type, and location (Region, City / Market), then gets adjusted by escalation and market factors. Total CAPEX divided by IT capacity gives Cost per kW, the industry benchmark; it also anchors every downstream financial metric — Equity IRR, DSCR, NPV, and Payback Period all start from this number.
total-capex.f: Total CAPEX = sum(construction + equipment + fit-out + soft costs) x location x escalation x market factors

cost-per-kw.d: The industry benchmark unit cost: Total CAPEX divided by IT Load capacity. Typical ranges are $8,000–15,000/kW for Tier III facilities and $15,000–25,000/kW for Tier IV; AI/liquid-cooled builds trend higher on mechanical scope but can be lower per kW at very high Rack Density because the building shrinks. Comparing your figure against the City / Market $/W anchors and Benchmark Percentile tells you instantly whether an estimate is credible.
cost-per-kw.f: Cost per kW = Total CAPEX / IT Load (kW)

tier-class.d: The Uptime Institute's four-level availability classification, determined chiefly by Redundancy topology: Tier I (N) = 99.671% availability, Tier II = 99.741%, Tier III (N+1, concurrently maintainable) = 99.982%, Tier IV (2N, fault tolerant) = 99.995%. Each tier step roughly means an order-of-magnitude less annual downtime but materially more CAPEX — Tier IV can cost 1.5–2x a Tier II per kW. Tier III is the commercial colocation standard; the tier you build should match the revenue and SLA model, not exceed it.

uptime-sla.d: The percentage of the year the facility is expected to be operational, set by the Redundancy level and Tier Classification. 99.982% (Tier III) allows about 1.6 hours of downtime per year; 99.995% (Tier IV) about 26 minutes; adding another nine multiplies infrastructure cost. Contractual SLA breaches typically trigger service credits, so the gap between designed availability and sold SLA is a real risk position quantified in the Risk Analysis module.

annual-energy-cost.d: Estimated yearly electricity spend: IT Load x PUE x 8,760 hours x the electricity rate. It is an OPEX item, not part of CAPEX, and over a 10–15 year horizon it typically exceeds the original build cost — which is why a 0.1 PUE improvement or an On-Site Renewable hedge moves TCO more than most construction savings. Feeds directly into NOI and therefore DSCR in the financing model.
annual-energy-cost.f: Annual Energy = IT Load (kW) x PUE x 8,760 h x $/kWh

deep-sea-water-cooling.d: Chiller-less primary cooling that rejects heat into cold deep seawater (4–6 °C drawn from 800–1000 m depth) through a Titanium Plate Heat Exchanger, organized as a Three-Loop Architecture (rack CDU → closed facility water → open seawater). Because the ocean does the refrigeration, compressor energy disappears: design PUE ≤ 1.15 and WUE ≈ 0 (no evaporative water use), with a Trim Chiller kept as hybrid backup for warm events and maintenance. Reference basis: a 150 MW AI data center rejecting 172.5 MW of heat needs 8.625 m³/s (31,050 m³/h) of Seawater Flow at the 5 °C design ΔT, moved by 4+1 pumps of 2.9 m³/s at 60 m head (~2,000 kW each).
deep-sea-water-cooling.f: Flow = Heat (W) / (rho x cp x deltaT); poster basis: 172.5e6 / (4000 x 1000/... ) -> 8.625 m3/s at deltaT 5 C
deep-sea-water-cooling.s: 150 MW AI DC deep-sea cooling reference architecture (2026); Makai Ocean Engineering SWAC studies; NOAA World Ocean Atlas temperature profiles

intake-depth.d: How deep the seawater intake sits, which sets the source temperature and therefore the whole cooling capability: typical tropical/subtropical profiles give ~4 °C at 1100 m+, 5 °C at 900 m, 6 °C at 700 m, 8 °C at 500 m, 11 °C at 300 m, and ~16 °C at the surface. The design target of 4–6 °C means intakes at 800–1000 m; going shallower saves HDPE Marine Pipeline cost but warms the source, shrinking the Titanium PHE approach margin and forcing more Trim Chiller hours. Depth also increases Pump Head via longer pipeline friction.
intake-depth.s: NOAA World Ocean Atlas typical tropical/subtropical profiles

seawater-delta-t.d: How much the seawater warms passing through the heat exchanger — the design value is 5 °C, which is also the common environmental discharge limit (ΔT ≤ 5 °C at the Outfall Diffuser mixing zone). ΔT and Seawater Flow trade off directly: halving ΔT doubles the required flow, pump power, and pipeline size, while pushing ΔT above the permit limit risks the discharge consent. The reference design moves 8.625 m³/s at exactly 5 °C to reject 172.5 MW.
seawater-delta-t.f: Q (heat) = rho x cp x Flow x deltaT

trim-chiller.d: A conventional chiller plant sized at a fraction of total load (design basis 35% capacity) that runs only during warm-water events, peak excursions, or seawater-system maintenance — roughly 300 hours per year in the reference design, at ~$260k per MWth installed. It converts Deep Sea Water Cooling from a single-point-of-failure bet into an N+1 hybrid: the ocean carries the base load, the trim plant guarantees the SLA. Because it runs so few hours, its Refrigerant choice (typically ultra-low-GWP R-1234ze) has minimal Scope-1 impact.

titanium-phe.d: The barrier between the corrosive open seawater loop and the clean closed facility-water loop, built from Titanium Grade 2 plates — the only mainstream material that survives decades of warm chloride exposure without pitting. Design approach temperature is 2.0 °C (range 1.5–2.5 °C): tighter approach means colder facility water but more plate area and cost (~$95k per MWth). Configured N+1 in parallel banks so individual units can be opened for cleaning without dropping the Three-Loop Architecture.

seawater-flow.d: The volume of seawater pumped through the system, fixed by physics: Flow = Heat / (density x specific heat x ΔT). The 150 MW reference (172.5 MW total heat with electrical losses) needs 8.625 m³/s = 31,050 m³/h at the 5 °C Seawater ΔT — comparable to a small river. Flow determines everything downstream: pump count and Pump Head, HDPE Marine Pipeline diameter, Seawater Filtration sizing ($260 per m³/h), and the Entrainment footprint at the intake.
seawater-flow.f: Flow (m3/s) = Heat (MW) x 1e6 / (rho x cp x deltaT); poster: 172.5 / (4.0 x 5) = 8.625 m3/s

pump-head.d: The total pressure the seawater pumps must develop, combining static lift (~15 m base) plus pipeline friction (~12 m per km of pipeline). The reference design uses 4 duty + 1 standby pumps rated 2.9 m³/s at 60 m head, roughly 2,000 kW each — pumping is the dominant energy user in a chiller-less system and the main term in its pPUE. Efficiencies stack multiplicatively (pump 0.87 x motor 0.96 x VFD 0.97 ≈ 0.81; poster basis uses 0.85 combined), so every point of pump efficiency bought at CAPEX time pays back for 25+ years.
pump-head.f: Pump power (W) = rho x g x Head x Flow / eff_total

ppue.d: PUE measured for one subsystem or zone rather than the whole facility — for Deep Sea Water Cooling, the cooling pPUE counts seawater pump power, facility-water loop pumps (~38% of seawater pump power), and CDU pumps (~10%) against IT load. Because there are no compressors, cooling pPUE lands far below chiller plants and holds the facility PUE at ≤ 1.15 (including ~5% electrical distribution losses). Comparing pPUE across subsystems shows exactly where the overhead watts go.
ppue.f: pPUE = (subsystem overhead energy + IT energy) / IT energy

three-loop-architecture.d: The separation of the cooling chain into three isolated hydraulic loops: the Technology Cooling System (rack CDU loop, direct-to-chip at 20–25 °C), the closed Facility Water System (clean treated water, ~10 bar design), and the open seawater loop. Each boundary crossing happens in a heat exchanger — the Titanium PHE at the seawater boundary — so corrosive, biologically active seawater never approaches the IT equipment, and a leak in any loop is contained. This layering costs approach temperature (each HX adds ~2 °C) but is what makes ocean cooling insurable and maintainable.

hdpe-marine-pipeline.d: The high-density polyethylene intake and outfall pipelines running from shore to depth — HDPE because it is corrosion-immune, flexible for seabed contours, and can be float-and-sink installed. Marine installation runs about 3x the onshore pipeline cost (industry range 2.5–4x); unit costs scale with flow, from ~$2.2M/km at ≤3 m³/s up to ~$7.5M/km at 20 m³/s, and the system needs 2 lines (intake + outfall) plus an intake structure (~$4.5M) and Outfall Diffuser (~$1.8M). Pipeline length to reach Intake Depth is typically the largest single CAPEX line in a Deep Sea Water Cooling build.

seawater-filtration.d: The multi-stage screening train that keeps marine life and debris out of the Titanium PHE: coarse 50 mm bars → fine 5 mm screens → traveling screens → 200 µm disc filters → 50 µm auto-backwash, configured N+1 so cleaning never interrupts flow. Sized at roughly $260 per m³/h of Seawater Flow (about $8M for the 31,050 m³/h reference). Filtration performance directly controls HX fouling rates and therefore Marine OPEX (cleaning frequency, chlorination dosing).

outfall-diffuser.d: The multi-port discharge structure (~$1.8M reference cost) that returns warmed seawater to the ocean while rapidly mixing it to meet the environmental limit — typically ΔT ≤ 5 °C at the edge of the mixing zone. Port sizing, spacing, and discharge depth are set by dilution modeling in the environmental permit; a well-designed diffuser is what keeps the thermal plume from stressing local ecosystems and keeps the discharge consent defensible. Paired with the intake structure at the other end of the HDPE Marine Pipeline.

entrainment.d: The drawing of small marine organisms — larvae, eggs, plankton — into the intake flow, the primary ecological concern of any large seawater system moving 31,050 m³/h. Mitigations include low intake approach velocities, deep placement (the 800–1000 m Intake Depth is naturally less biologically productive than surface waters), and fine Seawater Filtration screens with fish-return provisions. Entrainment and thermal-plume studies are core to the environmental impact assessment that permits the project.

n-plus-1-redundancy.d: One spare unit beyond the count needed for full load, applied throughout the Deep Sea Water Cooling design: pumps 4+1 (the +1 is design margin beyond the hydraulic minimum), filters N+1, Titanium PHE banks N+1 in parallel, Trim Chillers N+1, while power and controls run 2N. This lets any single pump, screen, or heat-exchanger be serviced with the system at full capacity — the marine equivalent of the electrical Redundancy that defines the facility Tier Classification.

marine-opex.d: The recurring cost of operating the seawater side: maintenance at ~3% of marine CAPEX per year, anti-biofouling chlorination dosing (~$6.5 per m³/h of flow per year), and annual ROV pipeline inspection (~$350k/yr). Pumps run at roughly 0.85 load factor, so pumping electricity is the other big line — together these replace the chiller maintenance and refrigerant costs of a conventional plant. Marine OPEX is usually well below the compressor energy it displaces, which is what makes the PUE ≤ 1.15 economics work over the asset life.

refrigerant.d: The working fluid in chillers and CRAC units, and a triple-impact choice: it drives cycle efficiency (COP), Scope-1 leakage emissions (via GWP), and safety-mitigation CAPEX (via the ASHRAE 34 Safety Class). Regulation is forcing the transition — the US AIM Act restricts GWP > 700 in new equipment from 2025 and the EU F-Gas Regulation targets GWP > 150 — pushing the industry from R-410A and R-134a toward A2L blends and ultra-low-GWP HFOs like R-1234ze. The calculator's 'Auto' mode picks the industry-typical refrigerant for the selected Cooling Type (e.g. R-410A for CRAC, R-134a for RDHX chillers, R-1234ze for Deep Sea trim plants).
refrigerant.s: GWP100 per IPCC AR4; ASHRAE Standard 34 safety classes

gwp.d: How many times more warming one kilogram of a gas causes than one kilogram of CO2 over 100 years (IPCC AR4 values used sitewide). Legacy refrigerants are heavy: R-410A = 2088, R-134a = 1430; transition fluids sit mid-range (R-513A = 631); next-generation options are near zero (R-1234ze = 7, R-290 propane = 3, R-717 ammonia = 0). GWP x annual leak rate x refrigerant charge gives the Scope-1 carbon from cooling, and GWP thresholds are the regulatory trigger — AIM Act bans GWP > 700 in new equipment from 2025, EU F-Gas targets GWP > 150.
gwp.f: Scope-1 leakage tCO2e/yr = charge (kg) x leak rate (%/yr) x GWP / 1000

ashrae-34-safety-class.d: The standard two-character refrigerant safety code: the letter grades toxicity (A = lower, B = higher) and the number grades flammability (1 = none, 2L = mildly flammable with low burning velocity, 2 = flammable, 3 = highly flammable). A1 fluids (R-134a, R-410A, R-1233zd) need no special mitigation; A2L fluids add ~3% equipment cost for leak detection and ventilation; B2L (ammonia) and A3 (propane) require machine-room isolation or strict charge limits, adding 6–7%. The class therefore converts directly into mitigation CAPEX in the refrigerant impact model.

a2l.d: The ASHRAE 34 class for refrigerants with low toxicity and mild flammability (low burning velocity, hard to ignite) — the class most of the industry is migrating to, including R-32, R-454B, and the HFO R-1234ze. A2L systems require leak detection, ventilation interlocks, and charge-limit compliance per ASHRAE 15/IEC 60335, modeled as a ~3% equipment cost premium. The trade is regulatory durability: A2L fluids clear the AIM Act and EU F-Gas GWP thresholds that are eliminating A1 legacy HFCs like R-410A.

b2l.d: The ASHRAE 34 class combining higher toxicity with mild flammability — in practice this means R-717 Ammonia, the zero-GWP industrial refrigerant. B2L systems demand dedicated machine-room isolation, gas detection, emergency ventilation, and occupied-space charge limits per IIAR and EN 378, modeled as a ~7% capex premium. The payoff is the best cycle efficiency in the database (COP index 1.04) with literally zero direct Global Warming Potential.

cop.d: Cooling delivered per unit of electrical input — a chiller with COP 6.5 (the water-cooled baseline in the engine) moves 6.5 kW of heat per kW of compressor power. Refrigerant choice shifts COP by a few percent either way (indexed to R-134a = 1.00: ammonia 1.04, R-32 1.02, R-410A 0.95, R-1234ze 0.96), which compounds over 8,760 hours a year into real PUE and Annual Energy Cost differences. Higher COP also shrinks the heat-rejection plant needed per MW of IT.

r410a.d: The dominant legacy refrigerant in DX CRAC units and packaged air conditioning — non-flammable A1, but with GWP 2088, among the worst climate profiles in service. The US AIM Act restricts GWP > 700 in new equipment from 2025 and the EU F-Gas phase-down is squeezing supply, so new builds should treat R-410A as end-of-life technology; R-454B is its designated successor in new DX equipment. Typical modeled leak rate 4%/yr with 0.15 kg charge per kWth — the highest Scope-1 leakage burden in the database.

r134a.d: The baseline centrifugal-chiller refrigerant (COP index 1.00 — everything else is measured against it), non-flammable A1 with GWP 1430. It remains common in large water-cooled chillers but is being phased down under the Kigali Amendment HFC schedule; R-513A is the low-GWP drop-in replacement (~3% capacity/efficiency penalty) and R-1234ze the clean-sheet successor. Typical modeled leak rate 3%/yr with 0.20 kg charge per kWth.

r513a.d: A lower-GWP azeotropic blend (GWP 631, non-flammable A1) designed as a drop-in replacement for R-134a in existing chillers, accepting roughly a 3% capacity/efficiency penalty (COP index 0.97). It is the pragmatic retrofit path: no equipment change, no flammability mitigation, and a 56% GWP cut — though it still exceeds the EU F-Gas GWP > 150 trajectory, making it transitional rather than final. New equipment increasingly skips straight to R-1234ze.

r1234ze.d: An ultra-low-GWP hydrofluoroolefin (HFO) with GWP 7 — effectively future-proof against both the AIM Act and EU F-Gas thresholds — used in centrifugal and screw chillers. It is mildly flammable (A2L, ~3% mitigation capex) with a small efficiency penalty (COP index 0.96) and a low 2%/yr modeled leak rate. It is the engine's auto-pick for Deep Sea Water Cooling Trim Chillers, where the few hundred annual run-hours make its near-zero climate footprint essentially free.

r717-ammonia.d: The zero-GWP industrial refrigerant with the best cycle efficiency in the database (COP index 1.04) and a century of industrial track record. Its constraint is toxicity: safety class B2L requires machine-room isolation, gas detection, and occupied-space charge limits per IIAR and EN 378, modeled as a ~7% capex premium. Compelling for large central plants where the machine room is remote from white space and the efficiency gain compounds across megawatts.

r290-propane.d: Natural-refrigerant propane: GWP 3, excellent efficiency (COP index 1.00), and the smallest charge requirement in the database (0.05 kg/kWth). The catch is class A3 — highly flammable — which imposes strict charge limits and confines it to outdoor or rooftop packaged units well away from occupied space, modeled as a ~6% capex premium. Attractive for modular outdoor chiller farms where the flammability zoning is free.

pue.d: The headline data center efficiency metric: total facility power divided by IT equipment power, so 1.0 is theoretical perfection and everything above it is overhead (mostly cooling, then distribution losses). Industry average sits around 1.55; efficient facilities run 1.2–1.4; best-in-class free-cooled or Deep Sea Water Cooling designs achieve below 1.2 (the DSWC reference designs to ≤ 1.15). Every 0.1 of PUE on a 10 MW facility is roughly 8.76 GWh/yr — PUE feeds straight into Annual Energy Cost, CUE, and the Carbon/ESG story.
pue.analogy: Like a restaurant where for every $2 of food served you also pay $1 for the lighting, AC, and refrigeration needed to serve it — that overhead ratio is a PUE of 1.5. A great kitchen gets the same meal out for 10-20 cents of overhead: PUE 1.1. The food (IT power) is what customers pay for; everything else is overhead to shrink.
pue.f: PUE = Total Facility Power / IT Equipment Power

wue.d: Liters of water consumed per kWh of IT energy — the water twin of PUE, driven almost entirely by evaporative cooling (cooling towers, adiabatic pre-coolers). Evaporative plants commonly run 1–2 L/kWh, which for a 10 MW site is tens of millions of liters a year; closed-loop, air-cooled, and Deep Sea Water Cooling designs achieve WUE ≈ 0 because nothing evaporates. Increasingly a permitting and ESG gate in water-stressed regions, reported alongside PUE and CUE.
wue.analogy: Like tracking how many liters of water your house uses per hour of air conditioning. Two houses can be equally cool, but one evaporates thousands of liters through a cooling tower while the other runs a closed loop and uses almost none — WUE puts a number on that difference.
wue.f: WUE = Annual Water Consumption (L) / IT Energy (kWh)

cue.d: The carbon intensity of the facility's compute: total CO2 emissions from energy divided by IT energy, equal to PUE multiplied by the grid's carbon intensity. Two identical 1.3-PUE facilities can differ 20x in CUE depending on whether the grid is hydro/nuclear or coal — which is why siting and On-Site Renewable procurement move carbon more than another PUE decimal. Core metric of the Carbon/ESG module alongside Scope-1 refrigerant and Generator Type fuel emissions.
cue.f: CUE = Total CO2 (kg) / IT Energy (kWh) = PUE x grid carbon intensity

dcie.d: The reciprocal of PUE expressed as a percentage: IT power divided by total facility power. A PUE of 1.55 equals DCiE 65%; PUE 1.15 equals DCiE 87%. It carries identical information to PUE but reads intuitively as 'what share of my electricity actually reaches the servers' — useful when presenting efficiency to non-technical stakeholders.
dcie.f: DCiE = (IT Power / Total Facility Power) x 100% = 100% / PUE

partial-load-pue.d: PUE measured at less than design IT load — and almost always worse than nameplate, because fixed overheads (transformers, always-on fans, UPS losses) spread over fewer IT kilowatts. A facility rated PUE 1.3 at full load may run 1.6+ at 30% occupancy, which is exactly the early years of an Occupancy Ramp; this is why modeled Annual Energy Cost should use load-dependent PUE curves, not the brochure number. Modular plant deployment (adding cooling and UPS blocks with load) is the standard mitigation.

white-space.d: The floor area that holds IT racks — the revenue-generating footprint, as opposed to Support Space (electrical rooms, cooling plant, corridors, loading). White space requirement falls as Rack Density rises: an AI hall at 50–100 kW/rack needs a fraction of the floor of a 5 kW/rack enterprise hall for the same megawatts. Colocation Pricing and facility economics are quoted per kW far more than per square meter precisely because power, not floor, is the scarce resource.

rack-density-kw-m2.d: IT power per square meter of White Space, combining rack power and rack spacing — legacy enterprise halls run 1–2 kW/m², modern colocation 2–4 kW/m², and AI/HPC liquid-cooled halls can exceed 10 kW/m². Higher density shrinks the building (cheaper shell per MW) but concentrates structural floor loading (liquid-cooled racks can exceed 1,500 kg) and cooling distribution. The engine's space model derives hall area from IT Load, Rack Density, and layout allowances.

support-space.d: All non-IT floor area: electrical rooms, UPS and battery rooms, cooling plant, generator yards, fuel storage, network entry rooms, corridors, loading docks, and offices. Support space commonly equals or exceeds the White Space itself — higher Redundancy (2N duplicates plant rooms) and on-site fuel for long Fuel Autonomy both inflate it. It earns no direct revenue, so efficient support-space ratio is a real design KPI in the space model.

dscr.d: Net Operating Income divided by annual debt service (principal + interest) — the lender's primary covenant metric answering 'how comfortably does the project pay its loan'. Data center project finance typically requires minimum DSCR of 1.20–1.40x, with hyperscale pre-leased assets achieving cheaper debt at lower thresholds; a DSCR below 1.0 means the project cannot cover its debt from operations. It is squeezed from both sides: NOI (via Occupancy Ramp, Revenue per kW, OPEX Growth) and leverage (via the Debt Ratio and interest rate), and it caps how much debt the Capital Structure can carry.

equity-irr.t: Equity IRR (Internal Rate of Return to Equity)
equity-irr.d: The annualized return on the equity slice of the capital stack, after debt service — the number sponsors and investors actually underwrite. Leverage amplifies it: if the Project IRR exceeds the cost of debt, raising the Debt Ratio lifts Equity IRR (and its risk); typical stabilized data center deals target low-to-mid teens Equity IRR, with development-risk deals in the high teens to twenties. Highly sensitive to the Exit EV/EBITDA Multiple, Occupancy Ramp speed, and Revenue per kW — the Sensitivity Matrix and Monte Carlo modules quantify exactly how much.
equity-irr.f: IRR: rate where NPV of levered equity cash flows (incl. Terminal Value) = 0

project-irr.d: The internal rate of return on total invested capital before any financing — the project's intrinsic economics independent of how it is funded. Comparing Project IRR against WACC is the go/no-go test (a 12% hurdle is a common data center screen); the gap between Project IRR and the cost of debt is what leverage converts into extra Equity IRR. Because it strips out capital-structure choices, it is the right metric for ranking sites in the Portfolio module.
project-irr.f: IRR: rate where NPV of unlevered project cash flows = 0

exit-ev-ebitda-multiple.d: The valuation multiple assumed when the asset is sold or refinanced at the end of the hold: Enterprise Value = exit-year EBITDA x the multiple. Stabilized data centers have traded in the mid-teens to 20x+ EV/EBITDA in recent cycles depending on tenant quality (Hyperscaler Pre-Lease commands premium multiples), market, and growth. Because the exit often represents the majority of total equity proceeds, Equity IRR is acutely sensitive to this single assumption — always stress it in the Sensitivity Matrix.
exit-ev-ebitda-multiple.f: Exit Enterprise Value = Exit-Year EBITDA x Multiple

debt-ratio-leverage.d: The share of Total CAPEX funded by debt rather than equity — data center project finance commonly runs 50–70% loan-to-cost, with stabilized refinancings going higher. More leverage magnifies Equity IRR when the project outearns its interest rate, but it also thins the DSCR cushion and raises default risk in downside scenarios; lenders size the loan to whichever binds first, the LTC cap or the DSCR covenant. The Investment module's Capital Structure and Debt Amortization Schedule show the mechanics.

occupancy-ramp.d: The year-by-year fill schedule from opening day to stabilized occupancy — typically 2–4 years for colocation, or nearly instant with a Hyperscaler Pre-Lease. The ramp shape dominates early cash flows: slow fill means years of fixed OPEX and debt service against partial Revenue per kW, depressed DSCR, and worse Partial-Load PUE. It is one of the highest-impact variables in the Tornado Chart, and editable per-year in the DCMOC financial model.

revenue-per-kw.d: The top-line pricing unit of the data center business: monthly (or annual) revenue per kW of contracted IT capacity. Retail colocation commonly achieves $100–250/kW/month depending on market and service level, while wholesale and Hyperscaler Pre-Lease deals run materially lower per kW but with long terms, built-in Escalation, and near-zero vacancy. Together with the Occupancy Ramp it defines revenue; against OPEX it defines NOI and EBITDA — it is a top driver in every Sensitivity Matrix.

opex-growth.d: The annual escalation rate applied to operating costs — energy, staffing, Maintenance, insurance — typically modeled at 2–4%/yr. The margin story lives in the spread between OPEX Growth and revenue Escalation: contracts that escalate at CPI while energy costs spike compress NOI and DSCR over the hold. Energy usually dominates the OPEX stack, so a power-price hedge or On-Site Renewable can matter more than every other cost line combined.

npv.d: The sum of all project cash flows discounted back to today at the discount rate (usually WACC), minus the initial investment — the direct dollar answer to 'does this create value'. Positive NPV means the project earns more than its cost of capital; the equivalent rate form of the same test is comparing Project IRR to the hurdle. Unlike IRR, NPV handles non-conventional cash flows cleanly and scales with project size, which is why the Financial module's Sensitivity Matrix reports both NPV and IRR per cell.
npv.analogy: Money later is worth less than money now — a million rupiah next year buys less than a million today. NPV converts every future cash flow into today's money and subtracts the investment; if the total is still positive, the project beats simply leaving the cash in the bank.
npv.f: NPV = sum( CF_t / (1 + r)^t ) - Initial Investment

payback-period.d: How many years until cumulative cash inflows recover the initial investment — the simplest capital-recovery metric. Data center builds typically pay back in 6–10 years undiscounted depending on Revenue per kW and Occupancy Ramp speed. Its weakness is ignoring the time value of money and everything after breakeven (including Terminal Value); use the Discounted Payback and NPV alongside it rather than instead of them.
payback-period.f: Payback = years until cumulative cash flow >= initial investment

discounted-payback.d: The payback calculation with each year's cash flow discounted at the cost of capital first — the honest version of the Payback Period, always longer than the simple one. It answers 'when has the project repaid its capital including the return that capital had to earn'. A project whose discounted payback never arrives within the horizon has negative NPV by construction.
discounted-payback.f: Discounted Payback = years until sum( CF_t / (1+r)^t ) >= initial investment

wacc.d: The blended required return across the capital stack: cost of equity weighted by the equity share plus after-tax cost of debt weighted by the Debt Ratio. It is the standard discount rate for NPV and the natural hurdle for Project IRR; data center WACCs commonly land in the 7–10% range depending on leverage, rates, and asset risk. Because debt is cheaper than equity (and interest is tax-deductible), leverage lowers WACC — up to the point where financial risk starts raising both components.
wacc.f: WACC = E/(D+E) x Re + D/(D+E) x Rd x (1 - tax)

cap-rate.d: NOI divided by asset value — the real-estate market's shorthand for pricing income streams, and the inverse cousin of the EV/EBITDA multiple. Stabilized data centers have traded at cap rates in the 5–7% range in recent cycles, tighter (lower) for long-leased hyperscale assets and wider for retail colocation with shorter contracts. Cap-rate movement between entry and exit is a silent but powerful driver of Equity IRR: 100 bps of expansion can erase years of NOI growth.

noi.d: Revenue minus operating expenses, before debt service, income tax, Depreciation, and capital expenditure — the clean measure of what the asset itself earns. NOI is the numerator of both DSCR (lender view) and the Cap Rate valuation (buyer view), making it the single most consequential line in the operating model. It is built from Revenue per kW x occupancy minus the OPEX stack, so the Occupancy Ramp and energy costs move it directly.
noi.f: NOI = Operating Revenue - Operating Expenses (before debt, tax, depreciation)

ebitda.d: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — the operating cash-generation proxy used for valuation (Exit EV/EBITDA Multiple) and leverage metrics (debt/EBITDA). For a data center it is nearly identical to NOI, differing mainly in corporate overhead treatment; stabilized facilities commonly run 50–65% EBITDA margins because the cost base is dominated by pass-through or contracted items. Exit-year EBITDA times the exit multiple is usually the largest single cash flow in the deal.
ebitda.f: EBITDA = Revenue - OPEX (before interest, tax, depreciation, amortization)

sensitivity-matrix.d: A grid that recomputes the model across simultaneous variations of two drivers — in the DCMOC Financial module, CAPEX variation (rows) against Revenue per kW variation (columns), with each cell showing NPV / IRR. It reveals interaction effects a one-variable-at-a-time Tornado Chart misses (e.g. high CAPEX is survivable only if revenue also lands high), and shows how close the deal sits to its breakeven frontier. The disciplined workflow: tornado to find the top two drivers, then a sensitivity matrix on exactly those.

monte-carlo.d: Thousands of model runs (the capex calculator uses 4,000, seeded and reproducible) with the uncertain inputs — construction bid spread, multi-year Escalation, scope growth, or in the DCMOC financial version revenue and cost drivers — drawn randomly from probability distributions each time. The output is a distribution rather than a point estimate, summarized as P10/P50/P90 percentiles: your Contingency should cover the gap between the point estimate and where P90 lands. Powered by RZEngine v2.0 in the capex calculator; the DCMOC Monte Carlo tab applies the same method to IRR and NPV.

tornado-chart.d: A ranked bar chart showing how much the output (Total CAPEX, NPV, or IRR) moves when each input swings across its plausible range, one variable at a time, holding the rest at base case — widest bar on top, hence the tornado shape. It answers the only question that matters in early-stage estimating: which two or three assumptions deserve real diligence money. In the capex calculator it ranks construction cost spread, escalation, and scope growth; pair it with the Sensitivity Matrix for the interaction view.

p10-p50-p90.d: Three points on the Monte-Carlo output distribution: P10 = only 10% of simulated outcomes come in below this (optimistic case), P50 = the median (most-likely), P90 = 90% of outcomes fall below it (conservative case — for a cost metric, only 10% of scenarios exceed it). Lenders and investment committees typically underwrite at P90 cost and P50-or-worse revenue; the P90/P10 spread is a direct measure of how uncertain the estimate really is. If your budget sits at P50 with no Contingency, you have roughly a coin-flip of overrunning.
table: Optimistic — 10% chance of coming in lower

capex.d: One-time investment in long-lived assets: land, building, electrical and mechanical plant, fit-out, and commissioning. CAPEX is capitalized on the balance sheet and recovered through Depreciation over asset lives (5–39 years by category), unlike OPEX which is expensed as incurred. The CAPEX/OPEX split shapes taxes, TCO, and financing — lenders fund CAPEX against future NOI, which is the whole project-finance construct.

opex.d: The recurring cost of running the facility: electricity (usually 40–60% of the stack — see Annual Energy Cost), staffing, Maintenance contracts, water, insurance, security, and property taxes. OPEX compounds at the OPEX Growth rate and, over a 10–15 year hold, typically exceeds the original CAPEX — which is why efficiency (PUE) and maintenance strategy dominate lifetime economics. Revenue minus OPEX is NOI, the engine of every valuation and coverage metric.

tco.d: The all-in lifetime cost of the facility: CAPEX plus the present value of every year of OPEX, refresh capital, and end-of-life costs over the analysis horizon (typically 10–15 years). TCO is the fair basis for comparing design alternatives that trade capital against operations — Deep Sea Water Cooling or a better PUE costs more up front and wins on TCO; a cheap build with poor efficiency loses. Discounting at WACC keeps the comparison honest across time.
tco.f: TCO = CAPEX + sum( OPEX_t / (1+r)^t ) over horizon

escalation.d: Contractual or assumed annual price growth applied to a cash-flow line — construction cost escalation (see Year Escalation, ~7% CAGR 2020–2025 decelerating toward ~3.3% by 2030), lease revenue escalators (commonly 2–3%/yr or CPI-linked in Colocation Pricing), and OPEX Growth. The spread between revenue escalation and cost escalation determines whether margins expand or compress over the hold, so model them separately rather than assuming one inflation number.

colocation-pricing.d: How multi-tenant data center capacity is sold: retail colocation prices per kW per month (commonly $100–250/kW/mo with cross-connects and remote hands on top), while wholesale prices per kW or per MW on multi-year terms at lower unit rates. Pricing power tracks market vacancy, power availability, and connectivity (a Fiber Entry meet-me room adds interconnection revenue). Contract Escalation clauses and term length determine how durable today's Revenue per kW is against OPEX Growth.

hyperscaler-prelease.d: A long-term lease (often 10–15 years) signed with a hyperscale cloud or AI tenant before or during construction, typically for the entire building. It transforms the risk profile: the Occupancy Ramp collapses to near-instant, lenders accept higher Debt Ratios at lower rates because DSCR is contractually visible, and exit buyers pay premium EV/EBITDA multiples for the covenant. The trade-off is lower Revenue per kW than retail colocation and concentration risk in a single credit.

tax-holiday.d: Government incentives that reduce or defer taxes for qualifying data center investments: corporate income tax holidays (Indonesia offers up to 20 years for large pioneer-industry investments), sales/VAT exemptions on equipment, accelerated Depreciation, and free-trade-zone benefits. Incentives can move after-tax Equity IRR by several points and materially shift country rankings — which is why the DCMOC Tax & Incentives module computes an effective tax-rate timeline and NPV-normalized incentive ranking per country.

depreciation.d: The accounting allocation of CAPEX over asset useful lives — building shell 30–39 years, electrical and mechanical plant 10–20, IT and controls 3–7 — via straight-line or declining-balance methods. It is a non-cash expense that shields income from tax (the depreciation tax shield), so accelerated schedules and Tax Holiday interactions pull real cash value forward. The DCMOC Asset Lifecycle module models category-level depreciation, book value decay, and replacement timing across the projection horizon.

terminal-value.d: The assumed value of the asset at the end of the explicit forecast, typically exit-year EBITDA times the Exit EV/EBITDA Multiple (or NOI divided by an exit Cap Rate — the same idea in real-estate form). It frequently represents 40–60% of total present value in a 10-year model, which means the 'answer' is heavily an assumption about the future sale market. Stress the exit multiple in the Sensitivity Matrix before trusting any Equity IRR.
terminal-value.f: Terminal Value = Exit EBITDA x Exit Multiple (or NOI / exit cap rate)

cash-flow-waterfall.d: The strict priority ladder by which each period's cash is distributed: operating costs first, then senior debt service (interest, then scheduled principal), then reserves and covenants, and only then equity distributions — often further split by sponsor/investor promote tiers. The waterfall is why DSCR matters: debt eats before equity does, so thin coverage years mean zero distributions even when EBITDA is positive. The Investment module's amortization schedule and coverage charts trace this ladder year by year.

benchmark-percentile.d: Where a metric sits relative to a reference population — for example, a Cost per kW at the 30th percentile of the City / Market dataset means 70% of comparable builds cost more. Percentile framing is how the DCMOC Benchmarks module scores countries across cost, energy, connectivity, talent, and risk categories, converting raw numbers into rankings a board can act on. Beware population definition: a 'cheap' P20 build against Tier IV comparables may be a P80 build against Tier II ones.

tab-sim.d: DCMOC's default operations-simulation view: models the facility's operating envelope including overtime and regulatory labor analysis (Indonesia PP 35/2021), environmental physics (power-law load/temperature effects), and risk-and-downtime exposure by Tier level. The launching point that feeds the Staffing, Maintenance, and Financial modules.

tab-staff.d: Models the operations headcount: detailed role breakdown with monthly costs, shift-pattern coverage, and a 5-year cost projection in USD. Staffing is a top-three OPEX line after energy, and Tier Classification drives minimum-coverage rules (24/7 shifts for Tier III+).

tab-maint.d: Plans preventive and corrective maintenance: event intensity by month (heatmap — darker means more events), per-system maintenance strategies with descriptions, and work-order views. Maintenance discipline is what converts designed Redundancy into actual Expected Uptime; deferred maintenance shows up later as Risk Analysis exposure.

tab-risk.d: Catalogs and scores operational risks — equipment failure modes, single points of failure, downtime exposure — with per-risk descriptions and mitigation status. Quantified downtime risk closes the loop between the engineering choices (Redundancy, Tier) and the financial model (lost revenue per outage hour).

tab-dashboard.d: The DC-OS executive dashboard — a single roll-up of every engine's headline output (capacity, CAPEX/OPEX, financial IRR, PUE/efficiency, reliability, risk, AI recommendations) for the current project. Every figure is engine-real, drawn from the shared rz-engine; the top tabs focus the view (Engineering, Construction, Operations, Financial, Analytics, Reports).

tab-report.d: Compiles the full analysis into an exportable report and lets you compare two saved scenarios side-by-side, including shift-model comparison recommendations. The executive-summary layer over every other module's output.

tab-capex.d: Configures the capital-cost model inside DCMOC — build cost per kW, phasing, and category breakdowns — with a generated narrative explaining the estimate. Mirrors the standalone capex calculator's logic and feeds Total CAPEX into the Financial and Investment modules.

tab-carbon.d: Models the facility's emissions footprint across scenarios: grid-electricity carbon (Scope 2, driven by PUE and grid intensity — see CUE), generator fuel and refrigerant leakage (Scope 1, driven by Generator Type and GWP), and decarbonization scenario descriptions. The ESG evidence base behind Green Certification and investor reporting.

tab-finance.d: The core project-finance model: cash flows, NPV and IRR, and a two-way Sensitivity Matrix of CAPEX variation (rows) versus Revenue per kW variation (columns) with NPV / IRR shown per cell. Where the engineering configuration becomes an investment case.

tab-invest.d: The levered view of the deal: Capital Structure (debt/equity split), the Debt Amortization Schedule, and the Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) tracked year by year against covenant levels. This is where the Debt Ratio, Equity IRR, and the Cash Flow Waterfall live.

tab-benchmark.d: Country-level benchmark analysis scoring markets across categorized criteria (cost, energy, connectivity, risk, talent) with per-category detail. Converts raw market data into Benchmark Percentile rankings for site-selection decisions.

tab-montecarlo.d: Runs a configurable Monte-Carlo Simulation on the selected country's financial model: adjust variable distributions, run thousands of trials, and read the outcome distribution as P10/P50/P90 bands for IRR and NPV. The probabilistic reality-check on the deterministic Financial tab.

tab-portfolio.d: Compares 2+ candidate sites side-by-side on a radar chart and metric table — import the current configuration or add blank site templates. The multi-site ranking view where unlevered Project IRR is the fair comparison basis.

tab-capacity.d: Plans phased capacity build-out: phase configuration, a build-timeline Gantt chart, and a narrative of when each megawatt tranche lands. Phasing matches CAPEX deployment to the Occupancy Ramp so capital is not stranded ahead of demand — Transformer Lead Time is usually the gating item.

tab-phased-finance.d: The financial model of the phased build: blended cash flow across phases and an investment decision matrix against a 12% hurdle rate, with narrative. Shows whether later phases stand on their own economics or ride on phase-1 infrastructure.

tab-tax.d: Models country tax regimes and incentives: a tax-rate timeline (standard vs effective under a Tax Holiday), free-trade-zone listings, and an NPV-normalized incentive value ranking. Effective-tax deltas of this size routinely re-rank countries in the Portfolio comparison.

tab-disaster.d: Natural-hazard exposure per country shown as a risk radar (earthquake, flood, typhoon, volcanic) with costed mitigation options. Complements the Seismic Zone input in the capex model — hazard drives both construction premium and insurance OPEX.

tab-grid.d: Scores utility-grid dependability by country and computes the annual grid-risk cost breakdown: outage frequency/duration converted into generator run-hours, fuel burn, and downtime exposure. Weak grids shift the design toward longer Fuel Autonomy and heavier Generator Type investment.

tab-talent.d: Scores the availability of qualified data center operations and engineering talent by country, with factor-level analysis. Talent scarcity inflates the Staffing cost model and construction-phase Contractor Availability premiums.

tab-compliance.d: Auto-generates the regulatory requirement checklist per country (Module 41) and scores compliance coverage — data-protection law, building and environmental permits, sector certifications — with per-item notes. Compliance gaps are schedule and licensing risk, not just paperwork.

tab-asset-lifecycle.d: Tracks every asset category through its useful life: category-level Depreciation expense per year (bar widths proportional to annual totals), declining book value versus cumulative replacement spend, and configurable depreciation method over the projection horizon. The refresh-capital planning view that keeps late-hold cash flows honest.

tab-cbm.d: Module 43 — evaluates BMS/DCIM sensor investment against failure-avoidance savings: sensor categories with count formulas, coverage economics, and payback. Condition-based maintenance replaces calendar-based Maintenance intervals with actual equipment health data, cutting both cost and surprise failures; intelligent PDU Type telemetry is one of its data feeds.

tab-fuel-gen.d: Module 44 — diesel generator sizing, fuel consumption, and cost modeling: liters per year at the modeled run profile, priced at each country's diesel price including tax. Connects Grid Reliability (how often generators run) with Fuel Autonomy (how much tankage) into an annual OPEX number.

tab-strategic.d: Long-horizon capacity strategy: projects demand growth against installed capacity and flags when expansion is needed within the planning horizon (or confirms none is). The bridge from a single-site Capacity Plan to a multi-year, multi-phase investment roadmap.

tab-faq.d: The in-app manual: explains each DCMOC module, its inputs, assumptions, and data vintage, with per-item descriptions. Start here to understand what each tab computes and which numbers are estimate-grade versus sourced.

ft-overview.d: The market-at-a-glance dashboard: major indices, top movers, sector snapshot, and headline economic prints in one view. The launch pad before drilling into Stocks, Sectors, or Economy tabs.

ft-stocks.d: Individual equity view: quotes, candlestick charts with technical indicators (RSI, moving averages, MACD), and the FIN Investment Committee scorecard combining Value Gate screening with conviction scoring. Covers US and Indonesian (IDX .JK) markets. Educational analysis only — not investment advice.

ft-forex.d: Foreign-exchange rates and history for major and Asian pairs (USD/IDR and peers), with charting. Currency moves matter directly to data center economics: CAPEX is largely USD-denominated equipment while revenue may be local-currency.

ft-crypto.d: Cryptocurrency market data with candle charts and a technical-only committee analysis (Technical + Quant + Risk panels) plus a momentum-scored crypto screener. Fundamentals are intentionally excluded — crypto has no earnings to value. Educational only, not investment advice.

ft-commodities.d: Prices and charts for energy, metals, and agricultural commodities. Energy commodities (natural gas, crude) and metals (copper, aluminum) are leading indicators for data center OPEX and construction costs respectively.

ft-screener.d: Filters the US or Indonesian stock universe by fundamentals and technicals, ranked by the FIN Engine composite score (value, quality, momentum, risk factors). The systematic top-of-funnel that feeds candidates into the Stocks committee analysis and your Watchlist.

ft-watchlist.d: Your saved symbols with live quotes in one tracking view — the personal shortlist built from Screener results and Stocks research. Pair with Alerts to get notified on price triggers instead of watching the tape.

ft-news.d: Aggregated market news headlines across equities, macro, and crypto. Headlines drive short-term price action; cross-reference against the Economy calendar to separate noise from scheduled catalysts.

ft-sectors.d: Performance heat view of the 11 GICS sectors (technology, energy, financials, utilities, etc.), showing where money is rotating. Sector breadth confirms or contradicts index-level moves on the Overview tab.

ft-economy.d: Macro indicators dashboard: rates, inflation prints, employment, GDP, and central-bank data. The macro regime sets the discount-rate backdrop — the same force that moves equity valuations also moves data center WACC and Cap Rate assumptions.

ft-futures.d: Index and commodity futures quotes — the 24-hour risk signal that trades before and after cash markets open. Overnight futures direction is the standard read on how the cash session will open.

ft-alerts.d: Price-trigger notifications on your chosen symbols: set a level, get alerted when it crosses. Turns the Watchlist from a page you check into a system that checks for you.

interest-rate.d: The annual cost of debt on the project's borrowings, set by base rates plus a credit spread reflecting project risk, sponsor strength and pre-leasing. It directly drives annual debt service — a 100 bps move typically shifts Equity IRR by several points on a levered data-center deal — and squeezes DSCR from the payment side. Fixed-rate or hedged debt trades certainty for a higher coupon; floating exposes the project to rate cycles.
interest-rate.f: Annual Debt Service ≈ Principal × CRF(r, n)

energy-management-system.d: A structured framework — codified by ISO 50001 — for setting an energy policy, baselining consumption, identifying significant energy uses, and driving continual improvement through measurable targets. In a data center the EnMS ties PUE tracking, metering hierarchies and operational controls into an auditable Plan-Do-Check-Act loop.

budget-usd.d: The total funding envelope the owner commits to deliver the project. In DCMOC it is predefined at the P80 commitment basis — the screening CAPEX P50 multiplied by 1.2 — so the budget already carries headroom for estimate uncertainty at early AACE classes. Editable: replace it with the board-approved figure once one exists.

design-margin.d: Extra headroom added on top of the best-estimate design and cost basis to absorb scope growth, estimate error, and market movement. In DCMOC the Design Margin writes straight into the CAPEX contingency percentage, so raising it moves the investment cost and the whole financial baseline. Typical screening values are 5–20% depending on estimate maturity.

workload-mix.d: The share of total IT load carried by each workload class — AI/GPU compute, storage-intensive, general compute, and network/others. The mix drives the facility profile: a GPU-heavy mix pushes rack density and liquid cooling, while a storage-heavy mix favors lower density and air cooling. DCMOC predefines the mix from the selected use-case profile; tick manual override to adjust.

peak-it-load.d: The highest instantaneous power the IT equipment draws — the sizing basis for the entire power chain (UPS, generators, switchgear) and the cooling plant, which must all carry the peak, not the average. DCMOC predefines peak equal to the base IT load; edit it if the design carries burst headroom above nameplate.

avg-it-load.d: The time-averaged power the IT equipment actually draws through the year — the basis for energy bills and OPEX, whereas peak load sizes the equipment. AI training clusters typically run at 70–80% utilization of peak, so DCMOC predefines average as 75% of peak; replace it with measured utilization when available.

total-racks.d: The estimated number of IT racks the facility must house, derived from the IT load and the average rack density. It sizes the data-hall floor area, containment rows, and structured cabling. DCMOC computes it automatically and lets you override to match the actual deployment plan.
total-racks.f: Total Racks = ceil(IT Load ÷ Average Rack Density)

deep-sea-depth.d: The depth of the cold-water intake for a deep-sea (or deep-lake) cooling loop. Deeper intakes reach colder, thermally stable water — around 60 m and below the supply is cold enough year-round to reject the full facility heat load without chillers, which is what enables the chiller-less PUE ≤ 1.15 basis.

pipeline-length.d: The run of intake and return piping between the facility and the deep-water intake point. It is the dominant civil/marine CAPEX item of a deep-sea cooling system and sets the pumping head the seawater pumps must overcome, so longer routes trade colder water against higher capital and pump energy.

loop-delta-t.d: The temperature rise of the water across the cooling loop — the difference between return and supply. A larger ΔT moves the same heat with less flow, shrinking pipe diameter and pump energy; a smaller ΔT needs more flow. It is the denominator of the fundamental flow equation for any water loop.
loop-delta-t.f: Flow (m³/s) = Heat (kW) ÷ (ρ × cp × ΔT) ≈ Q ÷ (4186 × ΔT)

take-or-pay.d: A contract clause obliging the buyer to pay for a minimum committed quantity — power capacity, cooling, or colocation space — whether or not it is actually consumed. Utilities and colo providers use it to de-risk the infrastructure they build for you; for the tenant it converts usage risk into a fixed obligation that must be covered by the ramp plan.

nrc.d: The one-time fee at the start of a colocation or connectivity contract — installation, fit-out, cross-connect setup, and commissioning of the customer space. Paid once, in contrast to the MRC that repeats monthly for the life of the term.

mrc.d: The fixed monthly fee in a colocation contract, usually quoted per kW of committed IT capacity or per rack, covering space, power availability, and cooling. Together with the one-time NRC it defines the tenant's cost structure; contract value ≈ NRC + MRC × term months.

p50.d: A cost or schedule estimate with a 50% probability of not being exceeded — the median outcome, with equal chance of coming in under or over. P50 is the honest central estimate, but committing a budget at P50 means a coin-flip of overrun, which is why budget commitments are usually set at P80.

p80.d: A cost or schedule estimate with an 80% probability of not being exceeded — the common budget-commitment basis, leaving only a 20% chance of overrun. At early screening classes P80 is approximated as P50 × 1.2; a formal Monte-Carlo risk analysis replaces that factor as the estimate matures.

aace-class.d: The AACE International classification of cost-estimate maturity, from Class 5 (concept screening, roughly -50%/+100% accuracy) down to Class 1 (definitive, around ±10%). The class tells you how much contingency and P50→P80 spread the estimate still needs — a Class 5 number is a direction, not a budget.

punchlist.d: The itemized list of defects, incomplete work, and deviations recorded during commissioning walk-downs and acceptance testing. Every item must be closed (or formally waived) before final acceptance and handover to operations — an open punch list is the practical gate between construction and revenue service.

newsvendor.d: A single-period inventory optimization that balances the cost of stocking too much (capital tied up in a part that never fails) against too little (downtime while a part ships). Used in DCMOC to size critical-spares holdings: stock up to the service level where the marginal underage and overage costs balance.
newsvendor.f: Optimal service level = Cu ÷ (Cu + Co)  — underage vs overage cost

spi.d: The earned-value ratio of work performed to work planned. SPI = 1.0 means on schedule, below 1.0 behind, above 1.0 ahead. Because it is measured in value rather than dates, it flags schedule slip early — while the milestone dates still look achievable on paper.
spi.f: SPI = EV ÷ PV (earned value ÷ planned value)

cpi.d: The earned-value ratio of work performed to money spent. CPI = 1.0 means on budget, below 1.0 over budget (each dollar buys less than a dollar of progress), above 1.0 under budget. CPI trends are stubborn — a project running CPI 0.9 at 30% complete rarely recovers to 1.0.
cpi.f: CPI = EV ÷ AC (earned value ÷ actual cost)

evm.d: The project-controls method that integrates scope, schedule, and cost in one measurement frame: planned value (PV) for what should be done, earned value (EV) for what is done, and actual cost (AC) for what was spent. From those three come SPI and CPI, plus forecast-at-completion — the standard dashboard for a build program.

saidi.d: The utility-grid reliability metric: average total outage minutes each customer experiences per year. A low-SAIDI grid means fewer generator starts and less fuel burn; a high-SAIDI grid pushes the design toward longer fuel autonomy and stricter backup testing. Used in DCMOC site intelligence to compare candidate grids.

pga.d: The maximum ground acceleration expected at the site during a design earthquake, expressed as a fraction of gravity (g). PGA sets the seismic design category, which dictates structural bracing, base isolation, and — often overlooked — the anchorage and snubbing of every rack, transformer, and pipe run.

water-stress.d: The ratio of total water demand to available renewable supply in the site's river basin (WRI Aqueduct scale, low to extremely high). A high-stress basin makes evaporative cooling a licence-to-operate risk — permits, community pressure, drought curtailment — and pushes the design toward dry coolers or liquid loops with low WUE.

irr.d: The discount rate at which the project's NPV equals zero — the annualized return the cash flows themselves earn. Decision rule: invest when IRR clears the hurdle rate (cost of capital + risk premium). IRR ignores project SCALE (a tiny project can post a huge IRR), so it is read together with NPV. Computed by bisection/Newton on the same cash-flow series as NPV.
irr.analogy: The effective 'interest rate' the project pays you, as if it were a savings account: a 15% IRR project is like a deposit earning 15% a year on the money you lock in. Compare it to your hurdle rate the same way you would compare deposit rates between banks.

pi.d: Present value created per dollar invested: (NPV + Investment) / Investment. PI > 1.0 means the discounted benefits exceed the capital; 1.08x reads as 8% value creation over the invested base. Useful for ranking projects when capital is constrained — but like NPV it depends on the discount rate used.
pi.analogy: Bang-for-the-buck: PI 1.3 means every $1 invested comes back as $1.30 of today's-money value. Like comparing promo deals by value per rupiah spent rather than by total size — a small project with PI 1.5 beats a giant one at PI 1.05 when capital is scarce.

blended-irr.d: Investment-weighted IRR across all build phases: each phase's IRR weighted by its share of total CAPEX. A phased campus can hide a weak phase inside a healthy blend — the per-phase decision matrix is the honest view. Adjusted for tax incentives, disaster-risk premium, grid-penalty OPEX, and talent-market costs before weighting.
blended-irr.f: Σ(phase IRR × phase CAPEX) / Σ(phase CAPEX)

payback.d: Years until cumulative net cash flow first turns positive. A screening metric only: it ignores the time value of money and everything after the payback point — a project can pay back fast and still destroy value (or slowly and create it). Use NPV/IRR for the decision; use payback for liquidity risk.
payback.analogy: How long until you get your money back. A fuel-efficient car costing Rp40jt more but saving Rp10jt of petrol a year pays back in 4 years. Simple and intuitive — but it ignores everything that happens after the payback date, which is its blind spot.

hurdle-rate.d: The minimum acceptable IRR for the investment — typically WACC plus a project-risk premium (construction, market, country risk). DCMOC's phased-finance verdicts compare IRR to a 12% default hurdle: below it a phase is NO-GO even with positive NPV, because capital could earn more at equal risk elsewhere.
hurdle-rate.analogy: Your personal 'not worth getting off the sofa' threshold. If a safe deposit already pays 6%, nobody accepts project risk for 7% — emerging-market projects must clear 18-25% before the risk is worth the trip. Below the hurdle, doing nothing is the better investment.

discount-rate.d: The rate used to translate future cash flows into today's dollars in NPV — the opportunity cost of capital. Usually set to WACC, plus premiums for country and project risk. Higher discount rate shrinks the value of distant cash flows: capital-heavy, long-payback DC projects are very sensitive to it.
discount-rate.analogy: The exchange rate between future money and today's money. Rp1jt promised next year is worth perhaps Rp900rb today — the discount rate is how steeply you mark down promises, and riskier promises get marked down harder.

idc.d: Financing interest that accrues on capital drawn before revenue starts — a real cost of the build period. Computed from each phase's draw schedule (monthly draws × construction loan rate × months outstanding) and capitalized into effective CAPEX. Longer schedules and front-loaded draws raise IDC; it is why schedule slip costs money even at fixed scope.
idc.analogy: The loan meter starts the day you borrow, but the building earns nothing during two years of construction — like paying a mortgage on a house you cannot live in yet. That 'meter running while the house is empty' is IDC, and it belongs in the real project price.

landed-cost.d: Equipment cost delivered to site: base price + import duty on the imported-equipment fraction + freight/insurance/customs. DCMOC applies the duty only to the imported-equipment share of each category (never to local labor), so high-duty countries raise electrical/mechanical CAPEX but not installation labor.
landed-cost.analogy: An online purchase from abroad: the $100 gadget becomes $150 after shipping, import duty, and the courier's handling fee. Budgeting transformers and chillers at ex-factory price repeats that surprise at million-dollar scale.

lcoe.d: Lifetime cost per MWh of an energy source: all discounted costs (CAPEX + OPEX + fuel) divided by discounted MWh produced. The comparison currency for solar vs wind vs grid: a renewable is economic when its LCOE (plus firming/storage) beats the delivered grid tariff. Sensitive to capacity factor and discount rate.
lcoe.analogy: Comparing a Rp30jt solar roof against monthly electricity bills is apples-to-oranges until you divide each option's lifetime cost by the lifetime kWh it delivers. LCOE is the honest price-per-kWh of every option on equal footing — like comparing cars by cost per kilometer, not sticker price.

bankability.d: Whether a project can attract debt financing on acceptable terms. Screening test: NPV > 0 AND IRR > WACC, plus debt-service coverage (DSCR ≥ ~1.25), contracted revenue quality, and counterparty/country risk. A technically excellent project with weak contracted cash flows is not bankable; lenders price the cash-flow certainty, not the engineering.
bankability.analogy: A mortgage application for a project: banks lend happily against a salaried job (a 15-year hyperscaler lease) and reluctantly against a freelancer's optimistic forecast (merchant colocation demand). Bankability is everything that makes the project look salaried in the lender's eyes.
