site-overall-score.d: Weighted composite of the site-intelligence pillars — tax incentives, disaster risk, grid reliability, talent availability, and compliance coverage — scored 0–100 for the selected country. It ranks LOCATION quality, not design quality: a low score means the country fights you (grid, talent, hazards), not that the design is wrong. Compare against the country-ranking chart before committing land.

availability-score.d: Site-level power availability outlook derived from the country grid profile (uptime, brownout frequency, outage duration) — how much the LOCATION helps or hurts your uptime target before any backup design. Weak grids are compensated with generation/BESS autonomy — at a cost the Grid Reliability tab quantifies.

connectivity-score.d: Screening view of network/fiber ecosystem quality for the country (subsea/IX presence, carrier depth, latency to major hubs). Directional only — validate against actual route diversity and dark-fiber availability for the specific parcel.

water-cooling-score.d: How friendly the location is to your cooling technology: climate (wet-bulb), water stress, and regulatory pressure on evaporative use. Low score + evaporative design = re-examine dry/liquid options; the Sustainability engine quantifies the water and PUE trade.

site-risk-score.d: LOWER IS BETTER. Location risk composite (natural hazards + grid + geopolitical screening) — 0 is a benign site, 100 a hostile one. Thin-green rendering means acceptable; drifting amber/red means insurance, structural adders, and downtime exposure rise. Click the value to trace the exact composition.
site-risk-score.analogy: A home-buyer's inspection summary: one overall grade built from many specific checks (roof, wiring, foundation). The grade is for ranking houses quickly; the checklist behind it tells you what you would actually need to fix.

disaster-risk-composite.d: LOWER IS BETTER. Weighted natural-hazard score: seismic 28% + flood 22% + typhoon 18% + volcano 12% + tsunami 10% + wildfire 10%, each hazard scored from the country profile (e.g. seismic zone 0–4 per USGS NSHM-class mapping). Drives the insurance multiplier, structural CAPEX adder, and expected annual loss. Mitigation levers lower the LOSS, not the score — the score is the location's nature.
disaster-risk-composite.analogy: An insurance adjuster's single glance at the property: earthquake, flood, cyclone, and fire histories folded into the one number that drives the premium. One figure for ranking sites — the per-hazard breakdown for deciding what to engineer against.

talent-index.d: Composite talent availability 0–100: DC-engineer pool depth, university pipeline, hyperscaler competition, hiring speed, certification density. Below ~55 = Difficult hiring (salary premiums, longer vacancies); below ~35 = Very Difficult (plan remote NOC, vendor O&M, or train-to-hire pipelines). The country comparison chart benchmarks alternatives.
talent-index.analogy: Like choosing where to open a restaurant partly by how many trained chefs already live nearby. A site with cheap land but no electricians and no BMS engineers within commuting distance pays the difference back in salaries, relocation packages, and vacancies.

hiring-difficulty.d: Categorical band of the Talent Index: Easy ≥70 · Moderate 55–69 · Difficult 35–54 · Very Difficult <35. A Very Difficult market does not block a project — it reprices it: salary premium, longer ramp, heavier vendor reliance. Click for the mitigation strategies and related workforce articles.
hiring-difficulty.analogy: Fishing in different lakes with the same rod: identical salary offers get very different catch rates by market. High difficulty means longer vacancies, higher offers to close, and more training from scratch — all real costs that follow from this one rating.

compliance-score.d: Framework coverage (60%) + mandatory-requirement readiness (40%) for the selected country — data-protection, energy-reporting, building/fire code exposure. Low score = more permitting friction and legal setup cost, not impossibility.
compliance-score.analogy: Like the hygiene rating in a restaurant window: one digit summarizing many inspections. A low score does not tell you which fridge failed — the underlying checklist does — but it instantly tells you which kitchens deserve a closer look.

results-overall-score.d: Capex-efficiency, sustainability, financial, and construction dimension scores, weighted into one 0–100 verdict with a grade. Read the four sub-scores before acting on the composite — a strong blend can hide one failing dimension.
results-overall-score.analogy: A decathlon score: one composite across ten disciplines lets you rank athletes instantly, but the champion can still be weak at pole vault. Read the per-dimension scores before betting the project on the headline number.

capex-efficiency-score.d: Your $/kW versus the regional benchmark band — 100 means at/below the efficient frontier for the tier and cooling class, lower means paying above market. Driven by tier/redundancy, cooling technology, region cost index, and scope choices.

sustainability-score.d: Mean of the four pillar scores — Energy (PUE band), Carbon (grid intensity × grid share), Water (WUE band), Waste (diversion). Each pillar has its own formula and its own levers; the composite is only as honest as its weakest pillar.

energy-score.d: (1.6 − PUE) / 0.5 × 100 — score ≥50 requires PUE ≤ 1.35. Moves with cooling technology, containment, economizer hours, and setpoint discipline. The EnPI page tests any efficiency claim behind this number.
energy-score.analogy: A school GPA for the site's electricity situation: tariff, grid reliability, and renewables folded into one grade. The GPA ranks candidates quickly — but read the transcript (the sub-metrics) before making the final decision.

carbon-score.d: (0.9 − grid intensity × grid share) / 0.9 × 100 — improves with cleaner grids or a larger renewable/PPA share. On a fossil grid the only real levers are contracted clean energy and efficiency; offsets are reporting, not physics.
carbon-score.analogy: Like checking where your tap water comes from rather than judging the tap: the socket looks identical everywhere, but the upstream grid mix makes the same kWh clean in one country and carbon-heavy in another. This score grades that upstream footprint.

water-score.d: (2.2 − WUE) / 2.2 × 100 — score ≥50 requires WUE ≤ 1.1 L/kWh. Evaporative cooling trades water for energy; dry coolers trade energy for water. Site water stress decides which trade is right.
water-score.analogy: Like checking a neighborhood's water pressure and drought history before opening a laundry business. A water-thirsty cooling design in a water-stressed region is the laundry with a dry tap — this score warns you before the lease is signed.

financial-health-score.d: 0.3 × budget-variance score + 0.35 × CPI + 0.35 × SPI, graded A–E. A single-source passthrough from Construction EVM — fix the schedule/cost performance there, not here.
financial-health-score.analogy: A doctor's overall verdict compiled from many vitals: blood pressure (DSCR), cholesterol (leverage), fitness (margins). One number is enough for triage; the panel of vitals is what you treat.

reliability-score.d: 40% availability-vs-tier + 30% redundancy depth + 15% maintainability + 15% SPOF exposure. A high score with a single-path utility intake is still fragile — read the SPOF list.

readiness-index.d: Weighted completion of the Cx program: L1–L5 checklists, IST/SAT/FAT evidence, punch-list closure — weights engine-real. 100% means turnover-evidence complete, not merely tests attempted.
readiness-index.analogy: A pilot's pre-flight checklist completion: what fraction of required items — staffing, spares, procedures, training — is ticked before you are cleared to carry passengers. 92% sounds fine until you notice the missing 8% includes the fuel check.

asset-health-index.d: Weibull remaining-life + condition + duty composite per class, fleet-weighted 0–100. Below ~50 with rising failure probability = replacement-planning territory — see the Replacement CAPEX Schedule.
asset-health-index.analogy: A used car's condition score combining age, mileage, and service history into one number. Good for ranking the fleet and budgeting replacements — but the mechanic's notes (per-asset findings) tell you which car actually needs the workshop first.

grid-grade.d: A ≥90 · B ≥75 · C ≥55 · D ≥35 · F below — from the grid score (uptime 40% + voltage stability 20% + brownout frequency 20% + outage duration 20%, blended 50/50 with the engine model). D/F does not forbid the site; it prices generation, BESS, and fuel autonomy into OPEX.
grid-grade.analogy: The reliability grade of your electricity supplier — the difference between a neighborhood with monthly blackouts and one with a blackout per decade. The worse the grade, the more of your own backup (generators, batteries, fuel) you must buy and maintain.
